composites.name: Biofilm Development — Draft Interface
composites.description: Fig 10.2 (panels c/d) — biofilm development as a hierarchical reorganization. Cells attach to a surface (SurfaceAttachment), the attached population secretes extracellular matrix (ECMSecretion), and the matrix-embedded community grows into a structured biofilm (BiofilmGrowth). All three processes act on leaves inside a single `biofilm` store nested in the environment — the individual cellular interfaces become part of a collective (biofilm) interface that couples, as one composite, to the surrounding environment. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no dynamics.

composites.name: Cell Disintegration — Coarse-Grained
composites.description: The Fig 6b grain-swap at the coarse grain, running: a lumped metabolism process turns substrate into biomass, energy, and secreted waste at fixed yields (with entropy production), beside the same molecular reaction network it coarse-grains. Identical interface to the draft — inert when run — but this handler advances the cell-level mass and energy budget rather than only naming it.

composites.name: Nested Molecular Hierarchy — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 8b nested hierarchy, running: six mass-action ODEs act on leaves deep in the place-graph — transmembrane transport, replication/repair, metabolism, transcription, translation, and ribosomal subunit assembly — advancing pools of DNA, RNA, protein, and metabolites in place. Same topology and wiring as the draft — inert when run — but this one moves matter through the central-dogma cascade (the real E. coli reactions run near ~45 nt·s⁻¹ and ~15 aa·s⁻¹; here at illustrative rates).

composites.name: Evolution — Draft Interface
composites.description: Fig 10.3 (panels e/f) — evolution reshapes the composition itself. Discrete driving events introduce variation (Variation), selection favors interfaces that sustain viability and fitness (Selection), and NEW interface capabilities arise through the ADDITION of a port (PortAddition). The environment holds several cell variants: an ancestral cell^ecoli and a derived cell^O157 that has gained an extra `new_port` (and `identity`) leaf its ancestor lacks — a new mode of interaction with the environment, not just a changed value. Evolution thus expands the space of possible organizations through new ports, couplings, and rewrites. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no dynamics (variation/port-addition described as driving-event rewrites in the contracts, not implemented).

composites.name: Cell–Environment Coupling — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 5b sense/act loop, running: reaction–diffusion, source/decay production, and mechanical relaxation evolve the shared chemical and mechanical fields while a single cell takes up nutrient, exerts traction, and updates its own mass, shape, and location. Same ports and wiring as the draft — which holds the fields fixed when run — but here the fields actually relax and the cell moves and grows in response.

composites.name: Cell–Environment Coupling
composites.description: Fig 5b — cell–environment coupling. Environmental processes (reaction–diffusion, production/degradation, mechanical stress) act on shared chemical and mechanical fields; the single cell senses those fields and acts back on them through uptake and traction, updating its own location, mass, and shape. This closes the minimal sense/act feedback loop. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no dynamics.

composites.name: Cell Division — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 10.1 division cycle, running: DNA replicates by ODE, chromosomes segregate toward the poles, and at the division time a rewrite handler partitions DNA and biomass into the two daughter stores and increments the cell count. Same ports as the draft — which describes division only as a contract and stays inert — but this one advances replication and fires the division event (see fig10-1-rewrite for live node addition).

composites.name: Cell Division — Live Topology
composites.description: Fig 10.1 as a GENUINE place-graph rewrite: chromosome segregation then cell division via Milner reaction rules over a tree[node] store. Running it ADDS nodes at runtime (1 cell -> 2 chromosomes -> 2 daughters) — steppable topology for the loom run/animate feature.

cycle.description: Cell-cycle length — time between chromosome-segregation + division events.

composites.name: Self-Organization & Coarse-Graining
composites.description: Fig 9a — self-organization, coarse-graining, and autopoiesis. Three functions — metabolism, containment, replication — each drawn at three grains, so that lumping a self-organized process (autocatalysis; membrane self-assembly; template replication) recovers its coarse closure. Read across, the three columns are autopoiesis: metabolism powers the boundary and the copying, containment concentrates both, replication reproduces the machinery they need. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no update dynamics.

composites.name: A Molecular Mechanism
composites.description: Fig 7b/7c — a molecular mechanism as a process with typed physical channels. Fig 7b: the molecular interface exchanges matter (chemical, mol·s⁻¹), charge (electrical, C·s⁻¹/A), momentum (mechanical, kg·m·s⁻²/N), and energy (thermal, J·s⁻¹/W), and is defined over molecular structure (PDB/SMILES) — no cell-level boundary. Fig 7c: the chemical channel refines into specialized subports — substrates, cofactors, catalysts, products. The mechanism is wired to a `ports` store (the typed channels + structure) and a `subports` store (the chemical refinement). DRAFT process: unit-bearing ports + behavior contract, no update dynamics.

composites.name: Self-Organization & Coarse-Graining — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 9a coarse-graining ladder, running: paired closure and fine-grained ODEs for each column — metabolism (far-from-equilibrium metabolite production vs. autocatalysis), containment (boundary assembly vs. membrane self-assembly and lipid aggregation), and replication (template maintenance vs. template-directed synthesis). Same ports and contracts as the draft — silent when run — but here every grain advances, so lumping a fine process visibly reproduces its coarse closure.

composites.name: The Cellular Interface — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 4b cellular interface, running: a single cell installed behind the exact ports the draft declared, growing by Monod kinetics on its sensed nutrient (half-saturation set in config) and losing viability as temperature departs its 37 °C optimum (±5 °C tolerance, Arrhenius-style thermal death). Same wiring as the draft — which stays inert when run — but this one actually grows, saturates, and dies past its thermal limit.

composites.name: Biofilm Development — Live Topology
composites.description: Fig 10.2 (biofilm) as a GENUINE place-graph rewrite: a founder cell colonizes (sibling cell nodes added one at a time up to capacity), then the mature community secretes extracellular matrix (an ECM node per cell). Running it ADDS place-graph nodes at runtime — steppable topology for the loom run/animate feature. The biofilm interface (a tree[node] community) grows from one cell into a structured multicellular collective.

capacity.description: Carrying capacity — how many cells the biofilm colonizes to.

grow_every.description: Time between cell-division events during colonization.

composites.name: Cell Division — Draft Interface
composites.description: Fig 10.1 (panel b) — division as a compositional rewrite. A prokaryotic cell replicates its chromosome (DNAReplication), segregates the copies toward the two poles (SegregateChromosome), and then splits — an event-driven graph rewrite (Divide) — partitioning state (DNA, biomass) into two daughters and incrementing the cell count. The daughters live as sibling stores under the shared environment, each re-coupling its own interface to it: division does not sever the coupling, it partitions the composition while the daughters remain coupled through the shared environment. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no dynamics (division/segregation described as event rewrites in the contracts, not implemented).

composites.name: The Cellular Interface
composites.description: Fig 4b — the minimal cellular interface. One cell (DRAFT process) senses environmental drivers and exposes physical exchange ports (chemical, mechanical, electrical, thermal) plus higher-level cellular ports (growth rate, shape, signaling, objective, viability). Chemical and mechanical ports refine into subports (named in the contract). All ports carry biological units.

composites.name: The Minimal Cell — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 9b minimal cell, running: four coupled cellular ODEs — containment (lipids→membrane), metabolism (enzymes+nutrients→metabolites+energy), gene expression (genes→proteins+enzymes), and replication (genes+energy→gene copies) — fed by generic diffusion and mass-action reactions over shared pools. Same shared-store wiring as the draft — inert when run — but here the pools actually flow, so metabolism's energy is spent by replication and expression's enzymes feed metabolism: autopoietic closure in motion.

composites.name: Cell Disintegration — FBA Metabolism
composites.description: The Fig 6b coarse metabolism running as flux-balance: bounded substrate uptake is allocated toward a capacity-limited biomass objective, yielding growth, energy, and secretion at fixed stoichiometry, beside the molecular reaction network it lumps. Same ports as the draft — which stays silent when run — but this one solves for the growth flux each step.

composites.name: Evolution — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 10.3 evolution program, running: variation perturbs the cell variants, selection reweights them toward viability and fitness, and a port-addition handler ramps the derived variant's new capability up to capacity. Same variant stores and ports as the draft — which names these as driving-event rewrites and stays inert — but this one actually drives variation, selection, and the emergence of the added port (see fig10-3-rewrite for live node add/remove).

composites.name: Interaction Modalities
composites.description: Fig 4a — four interaction-modality cards of the cellular interface: nutrient exchange (chemical flux), motile force (mechanical), growth rate, and electrical signaling. Each is a DRAFT process: unit-bearing ports + a behavior contract, no update dynamics. Ports are wired to labeled stores so each quantity (and its unit) appears as a node.

composites.name: The Minimal Cell
composites.description: Fig 9b — the minimal cell: the three columns of Fig 9a wired into one composite. Four processes — containment (lipids→membrane), metabolism (enzymes+nutrients→metabolites+energy), gene expression (genes→proteins+enzymes), and replication (genes+energy→gene copies) — are coupled through shared pools, with generic diffusion and mass-action reactions keeping the building-block stores supplied. Metabolism powers replication and expression supplies metabolism's enzymes: this mutual dependence through shared components is the minimal form of autopoietic closure. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no update dynamics.

composites.name: A Molecular Mechanism — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 7 molecular mechanism, running: a structure-defined transducer that moves matter (mol·s⁻¹), charge (A), momentum (N), and energy (W) across its four typed channels, driven by catalysis, conductance, mechanical coupling, and thermal-dissipation rate constants. Same channels and structure ports as the draft — which stays silent when run — but this one actually exchanges the four conserved currents each step.

composites.name: Biofilm Development — Executable
composites.description: The Fig 10.2 biofilm program, running: cells attach to the surface (adhesion-weighted), the attached population secretes extracellular matrix, and the matrix-embedded community accrues mass and grows — all acting on leaves inside the nested biofilm store. Same collective interface as the draft — inert when run — but this one advances attachment, secretion, and growth over time (see fig10-2-rewrite for live node addition).

composites.name: Cell Disintegration
composites.description: Fig 6b — cell disintegration as a grain-swap equivalence. A cell-level coarse-grained metabolism process and a molecular catalyzed-reaction network realize the SAME external interface at two different grains of description: coarse ⇄ fine. Lump the closed catalytic loops of the reaction network and you recover the coarse metabolism process; disintegrate the coarse process and you recover the network. Both grains are shown side by side, each wired to its own store cluster. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no update dynamics.

composites.name: Evolution — Live Topology
composites.description: Fig 10.3 (evolution) as a GENUINE place-graph rewrite: a wildtype population establishes (organism nodes added), a fitter MUTANT arises, then a selection sweep adds mutant offspring and prunes wildtype until the mutant lineage takes over. Running it ADDS and REMOVES place-graph nodes at runtime — steppable topology for the loom run/animate feature.

mutate_at.description: Time at which the fitter mutant lineage first appears.

composites.name: Cell Disintegration — Kinetic Metabolism
composites.description: The Fig 6b coarse metabolism running as Michaelis–Menten kinetics: substrate is consumed at a vmax/km-saturating rate into biomass, energy, and secreted waste, beside the molecular reaction network it lumps. Same interface as the draft — inert when run — but this one turns the enzyme-saturation curve into an advancing mass and energy budget.

composites.name: Nested Molecular Hierarchy
composites.description: Fig 8b — molecular compositions as a nested hierarchical composite. Molecular structure is organized as a nested place-graph across scales: an extracellular matrix, a membrane, and a cytoplasm containing a nucleus (chromosome → chromatin → nucleosome → DNA/histone), organelles (a ribosomal complex, mitochondria, secretory organelles), and cytoplasmic pools (proteins, RNA, enzymes, metabolites, nutrients). Six DRAFT processes act on leaves deep inside this hierarchy — transmembrane transport across the membrane, replication/repair and transcription in the nucleus, metabolism and translation in the cytoplasm, and assembly of subunits into the ribosomal complex — so the topology reads like Fig 8b. All DRAFT processes: unit-bearing ports + behavior contracts, no dynamics.
